items.title: ‘In gloomy 2013, I was spellbound by these characters’: Tracking down the 20-year-olds of a 1967 India
items.summary: Chapter 1: MIDNIGHT’S GROWN-UPS •2015 For most of last year, practically every fortnight, I dialled a house in Troy, Michigan, trying to speak to a man I had seen in a film half a century old. Let me admit, up front, that I failed. T.N. Subramaniam was unwell when I first called, his wife told me, and if he ever recovered enough for us to have a conversation, I never learned of it; abruptly, in August, his home turned unreachable, the phone ringing endlessly away. No one called back. After months of searching for Subramaniam and thinking about him, I lost my chance to ask him the questions that had gathered, like giant snowdrifts, in my mind. My obsession with the film he was in, I Am 20, began in the early autumn of 2013—a dispiriting season for India, a season vacant of cheer or promise. There had been a parade of bad news: outsized corruption, a gummed up economy, politicking of wearying vileness. An uninspiring election was drawing nearer. The nation’s affairs felt soiled and beleaguered, and the very project of India seemed to have gone awry in some profound way. In this troubled climate, I watched I Am 20 for the first time, and then dozens of times more, spellbound by its characters and by the messages it held. To be sure, I couldn’t easily have seen it before then. Commissioned by the state-run Films Division in 1967, it had kicked around as a filler in cinemas and then for a while on television; only in September 2013, when the Films Division posted a batch of its old productions on YouTube, did I Am 20 become widely available. I can’t remember how I stumbled upon it—following some trail from social media, no doubt—but I do recall the way my skin prickled in recognition. Here were our thoughts and deep worries of today, but fixed on film forty-six years earlier. What sorcery of repetitive history was this? items.title: Should not be a proxy war: Bombay High Court on MVA government reopening case against Arnab Goswami
items.summary: Legal proceedings should not become a “proxy kind of war”, the Bombay High Court said on Friday while hearing a petition filed by Republic TV Editor-in-Chief Arnab Goswami over his 2020 arrest by Maharashtra Police [Arnab Goswami v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.] Goswami filed the plea in 2020 seeking quashing of the FIR registered against him in 2018 at Alibaug Police Station, accusing him of abetting the suicide of interior designer Anvay Naik. During the hearing on Friday, Chief Public Prosecutor Shishir Hiray informed the bench that while a closure report was filed in the case, it was subsequently reopened in 2020. Advocate Niranjan Mundargi, appearing for Goswami, said that the State had reopened the investigation on its own volition without judicial authority, driven by political vendetta. He was referring to the earlier Maha Vikas Aghadi government which was in power in the State in 2020 when the case was reopened and he was arrested. Justice Milind Jadhav took note of the submissions and narrowed the primary legal issue to the scope of State power in reopening closed cases. "The question is whether the state has power to re-open and in what circumstances... This should not be a proxy kind of a war. We have a very healthy democratic state. There is a voice of dissent. We have four pillars of democracy and that would be the obvious desirable for the proper functioning of the democracy," Justice Jadhav remarked. Justice Milind Jadhav The judge also remarked on the judiciary’s unique position in such disputes. "We don't make the laws. We are not the elected representatives. Neither are we the media who are like a watchdog. We are the cementing authority between all three," he said. The Court also observed that “much water has flown since 2020” and suggested both parties to look at the case with a fresh perspective. The plea is likely to be heard next on September 4. Arnab Goswami was arrested in November 2020 in connection with the 2018 suicide of interior designer Anvay Naik, director of Concorde Designs Pvt Ltd (CDPL). Goswami argued in his petition that repeated attempts were made to clear the balance, but CDPL's inoperative bank account prevented settlement. items.title: Telangana citizens’ group seeks school fee regulation Bill in upcoming Assembly session
items.summary: The Telangana People’s Front, a citizens’ group comprising former bureaucrats, academics, activists and working professionals, has urged the state government to introduce and pass the Telangana Private Unaided School Fee Regulatory and Monitoring Commission Bill in the upcoming Assembly session. Speaking at a round-table meeting on school fee regulation and strengthening public education on Thursday, August 14, former IAS officer and Telangana People’s Front member Akunuri Murali said the Telangana Education Commission had submitted a draft of the Bill to the state government in January 2025, but no action had been taken since. Murali was the chairperson of the Telangana Education Commission when the draft was submitted. “We felt that we need to work as a pressure group, work with parents, and make it an election agenda to make this happen,” Murali said. He cited data from the Union Education Ministry’s Unified District Information System for Education (UDISE) Plus 2025-26 report to highlight the growing dependence on private schools despite high fees, which he attributed to inadequate funding and infrastructure in government schools. Telangana has 41,762 schools, according to the latest UDISE Plus data. Private unaided recognised schools account for around 32% of the total. However, 65% of the state's nearly 77 lakh students from pre-primary to Class 12 are enrolled in private schools. The proportion of students attending private schools has increased from 60% in 2023-24 to 65% in 2025-26, even as the number of private schools has declined by more than 1,100 during the period. The shift towards private schools is also evident among new entrants to the education system. Of the 6.4 lakh students admitted to Class 1 in Telangana in 2025-26, around 70% were enrolled in private schools, according to UDISE Plus data. Murali also pointed to the state of government schools, noting that nearly 82% of primary schools in Telangana have multi-grade teaching, where a single teacher teaches students from different grades in the same classroom simultaneously. The Telangana People’s Front has called on the government to immediately approve and implement the proposed Telangana Private Unaided School Fee Regulatory and Monitoring Commission Bill.
